Fugu/ puffer poisoning marks3
Pufferfish poisoning • Tetrodotoxic poisoning occurs following the ingestion of pufferfish, boxfish or
porcupine fish. • This is also known as puffer or fugu poisoning. • The poisoning is due to toxin known
as tetrodotoxin which is concentrated in the internal organs such as liver, ovary and intestines. • The
skin also contains some glands which secrete these toxins. • Usually the body muscles are free of the
toxin.

Lateral line systems marks3
The lateral line system in fish is an important sensory organ. It helps fish detect vibrations and
movements in the surrounding water. The system consists of a network of small canals called lateral
lines that run along the sides of the fish's body. Inside these canals are sensory cells called neuromasts,
which are sensitive to changes in water pressure. The lateral line system plays a crucial role in helping
fish navigate, find prey, and avoid predators.

       jaws.

   •   They possess paired appendages, such as pectoral and pelvic fins, which aid in movement and
       control.
   •   Unlike bony fish, Chondrichthyes do not have an operculum, a bony flap covering the gills.

what you know about chondrostean marks5
Chondrosteans are a group of ancient ray-finned fish with a cartilaginous skeleton. They are known for
their distinctive ganoid scales, which are thick and diamond-shaped.

Chondrostean are thought to be the most primitive of the ray-finned fishes. • They were at their greatest
diversity during the Paleozoic and Mesozoic eras. • Ancestral chondrosteans had a bony skeleton, but
living members, the sturgeons and paddlefishes, have cartilaginous skeletons. • Chondrosteans also have
a tail with a large upper lobe. • Most sturgeons live in the sea and migrate into rivers to breed. • (Some
sturgeons live in freshwater but maintain the migratory habits of their marine relatives.) • They are
large (up to 1,000 kg), and bony plates cover the anterior portion of the body. • Heavy scales cover the
tail. • The sturgeon mouth is small, and jaws are weak. Sturgeons feed on invertebrates that they stir up
from the sea or riverbed using their snouts. • Because sturgeons are valued for their caviar (eggs), they
have been severely overfished.

  Fish Sampling for Identification
  Collection of Specimens:

In order to collect the specimen, one must have the knowledge of all possible geographic
information of the surveyed place, including the distribution of various types of
vegetation, altitudes, seasons, means of transport, lodging, etc. However, main emphasis
should be given to the basin concept not to the political boundaries of the aquatic system.
It is also necessary to examine the previous collection of the concerned group to know
the various localities of the
already collected materials. The collection should be made from all zones of water body,
including surface, bottom, middle, upstream, midstream and downstream.
Methods of Collection: There are numerous methods to collect fish specimens round
the year. Fishes were collected using nets, traps, hooks and lines, electro-fishing
equipment, hand picking, buying from local fisherman and from local markets, etc.

Data Collection: The specimens which are being collected must bear collection data. A
specimen without such data is completely useless for a taxonomist. Thus, every specimen
collected must be labeled having the following data:

Geographical Location: Country, state, village, drainage basin, name of river, lake, etc.
A fish taxonomist should have a rich knowledge of the drainage concept. Some fish are
endemic to a particular basin and they are not found in another basin.
Name of the Collector: Name of the fisherman, scientist,
etc.
Coordinates: To be noted using GPS
Colour: Colour of the specimen in fresh should be noted.
Fixation and Preservation: The collected specimens should be first fixed in the
preservatives (10% formalin or 70% ethanol) in a large container so that the specimen
maintains its original shape after fixation. Preservation in tight containers distorts the
shape. Fishes may also be
Preserved in buffered 10% formalin. Buffered formalin is prepared by adding three
grams of borax per litre of 10% formalin solution. It retards the tissue shrinkage and
prevents decalcification of the tissue. A general rule is maintained not to have more than
40% of biomass per container of formalin during fixation (Figure 1).
After fixation the specimens are put in a glassstoppered bottles or screw capped jars with
the snout pointing downwards and then filled with freshly prepared preservative. An
incision should be made on the abdominal wall of the fish length 10-30 cm to one side
of the mid-ventral line with a scalpel knife or scissor. And for the fish longer than 30 cm
undiluted concentrated formalin is injected with the help of a hypodermic syringe
throughout the abdomen (Figure 1).

Tissue Sampling: Fresh tissue in the form of muscle, fins, etc. are collected from certain
specimens and preserved in ethanol for molecular studies.

Morphometric and Meristic Characters:
Morphometry refers to body proportions and meristics to counts.
Measurements were made point to point on the left             side   of    the         specimen
whenever possible.
Proportion of body parts are expressed in per cent of standard length and parts of head
in head length. Counts include fin rays: soft, hard, spinous, simple and branched;
lateral line: longitudinal and transverse; predorsal scales, circumferential and
circumpeduncular scales; branchiostegal rays, gill rakers, pharyngeal teeth, vertebrae,
etc. counts    and     measurements usually follow Kottelat unless it is modified by
different workers for particular genus or family for convenience. The reading should be
entered in a data sheet.

Osteology: Osteological data were taken from cleared and Alzarin stained specimens.
Disarticulations of bones, without damaging their structure, are done by treating the fresh
specimens directly in 2% KOH solution without any preservative. The specimens are
suspended in the solution      for    5-7     days    to      facilitate         the     natural
decomposition of muscle and ligaments. Addition of preservatives should be avoided

since it caused hardening of these tissues, which result in the damage of the bones at
their sutures at the time of manual separation. After this treatment, the bones are stained
with Alzarin. The stained bones are preserved in glycerine solution            or    10%
formaldehyde buffer solution. Identification of bones was based on Prokofiev. Rare
specimens are not dissected. Instead, radiographs may be taken for osteological studies.

Cataloguing of Specimens: The entries usually followed in cataloguing are consecutive
museum number, scientific name, locality, date and collector. The entire specimen
collected from one locality or district by one expedition are catalogued together. The
specimens are usually catalogued after they are identified at least up to genus level.The
museum register must have at least the following information (Table 1).
Comparison with the Nearest Congeners: The specimen under examination is
compared with its congeners. Firstly, they are compared with the species from the same
basin and then with the species of the same genus, the comparison is normally done with
the type specimen from their respective type locality. The best means to identify the
specimen is the direct comparison. When the literature on a species is not available, a
specimen is compared with the already identified one. This approach is useful at any
level. The type specimens are the most authentic at all. The original verbal descriptions
of specimens are the permanent records of the attributes of a given species.

  7. Neuromasts (for detecting water movements)

Fish have well-developed eyes adapted to see clearly in water. Their eyes are typically spherical,
allowing better focus and depth perception in aquatic environments. Many fish can see in color, and
some can even detect ultraviolet light.

Function:
The eyes help fish detect movement, identify prey and predators, and navigate their environment
visually, especially in well-lit areas.

The inner ear of fish is located deep within the head and contains structures such as semicircular canals
and otoliths. It is not visible externally.

Function:
It is responsible for both balance and hearing. Otoliths detect sound vibrations and changes in body
position, helping the fish maintain equilibrium and respond to underwater sounds.

The lateral line is a visible line of sensory pores running along both sides of a fish’s body from head to
tail. It contains specialized sensory cells.

Function:
It detects vibrations, water currents, and nearby movements. This system helps fish avoid obstacles,
detect predators, and stay coordinated in schools.

Fish have a pair of nostril-like openings called nares on each side of their snout. These lead to internal
olfactory sacs lined with sensory cells.

Function:
They are used for detecting chemical substances in water (smelling). This helps in locating food, sensing
danger, identifying mates, and navigating during migration.

Taste buds in fish are located not only in the mouth but also on external surfaces such as the lips, fins,
skin, and barbels (whisker-like structures).

Function:
They allow fish to detect the taste of substances in the water or on surfaces. This helps them identify and
evaluate food before consuming it, especially in dark or murky conditions.

These are specialized sensory pores filled with a jelly-like substance, primarily found in sharks and rays.
They are located on the snout and head.

Function:
They detect weak electric fields produced by the muscle movements of other animals. This enables the
fish to locate prey hidden in the sand and navigate using Earth's magnetic field.

Neuromasts are tiny hair cell clusters located within the lateral line and on the skin of some fish. They
are the primary sensory units of the lateral line system.

Function:
They detect the direction and strength of water movement. This helps fish sense nearby objects, react to
environmental changes, and maintain spatial awareness.

Step 2: Light is Focused by the Lens

The spherical lens bends the light to focus it onto the retina. In fish, the lens moves forward or backward
to adjust focus.

Step 3: Light is Detected by Photoreceptors

The retina contains rod cells (for dim light) and cone cells (for color and sharp vision), which detect the
incoming light.

Step 4: Conversion to Electrical Signals

The photoreceptors convert light into electrical nerve impulses.

Step 5: Transmission to the Brain

These impulses are sent through the optic nerve to the brain, where the visual information is processed.

Step 1: Sound and Movement Cause Otoliths to Shift

Sound waves or body movements cause the otoliths (calcium carbonate crystals) in the inner ear to
move.

Step 2: Bending of Hair Cells

The movement of otoliths causes nearby hair cells with cilia to bend inside the fluid-filled chambers.

Step 3: Creation of Nerve Impulses

The bending of cilia stimulates nerve endings, creating electrical signals.

Step 4: Signal Sent to Brain

The impulses travel to the brain via auditory nerves and are interpreted as sound and balance

Step 1: Water Movement is Detected

When fish or nearby objects move, they create vibrations and pressure waves in the water.

Step 2: Vibration Reaches Neuromasts

These vibrations enter the canals of the lateral line, reaching neuromasts that contain sensory hair cells.

Step 3: Hair Cells Bend

The water movement deflects the gelatinous cupula covering the hair cells, causing them to bend.

Step 4: Electrical Signal is Generated

The bending of hair cells triggers electrical impulses.

Step 5: Information is Sent to Brain

The signals are transmitted through nerves to the brain, allowing the fish to detect movement, avoid

A5. Museum labels should contain information about the exact locality, coordinates,
nearest landmark, date of collection, name of collector and any additional ecological
data related to the specimen.

habitat?
A6. Rohu fish has gills, heart, swim bladder and other organs to help it breathe, float,
digest food etc. It also has mucus glands, scales, fins and tail that aids its movement
and adaptation in the aquatic environment. The lateral line sense organs help it locate
prey and sense surroundings.

Q7. What are the different regions of fish skull in Labeo rohita?
A7. The four regions of skull in Labeo rohita are:
1) Ethmoidal region
2) Orbito temporal region
3) Otic region
4) Occipital region

Q8. Differentiate between the exoskeleton and endoskeleton of Labeo rohita.
A8. Exoskeleton comprises of scales and fin rays that provide outer covering and
support. Endoskeleton forms the internal bony framework and includes skull,
vertebral column, ribs and girdles.

Q9. What are the different water quality parameters tested to determine health
of water bodies?
A9. The different water quality parameters tested are:
1) Physical parameters like temperature, color, turbidity etc.
2) Chemical parameters like pH, dissolved oxygen, hardness, BOD, COD etc.
3) Biological parameters indicating microorganisms like bacteria, algae etc.

Q10. What are some natural and anthropogenic factors affecting water quality?
A10. Factors affecting water quality include:
- Atmospheric pollution
- Runoff
- Erosion and Sedimentation
- Discharge of domestic and industrial waste

Q11. Why is dissolved oxygen an important indicator of water quality?

A11. Dissolved oxygen concentration indicates the degree of pollution in water
bodies. Lower DO levels imply poorer water quality and high microbial activity due
to excessive waste.

Q12. How can turbidity affect the usage of water?
A12. High turbidity makes water aesthetically unappealing, reduces ability of light
to pass through water and affects processes like disinfection. It also indicates presence
of suspended impurities.

Q13. What are the structures present under each gill cover of fish?
A13. Under each gill cover there are four gill arches. Each gill arch has gill filaments
on the outside and gill rakers on the inside.

Q14. Which system did the pectoral and pelvic fins of fish evolve into in the first
tetrapods?
A14. Pectoral fins evolved into the front legs and pelvic fins evolved into the hind
legs of primitive tetrapods.

Q15. What is the function of mucus coating on skin of fish?
A15. Mucus coating helps reduce friction and provides protection to the fish skin
from abrasion and water flow.

Q16. What is the basin concept that should be considered while collecting fish
specimens?
A16. The basin concept emphasizes studying the geographical distribution of aquatic
systems based on drainages and basins rather than political boundaries. This provides
a more accurate ecological picture.

Q17. Name the different types of fishing crafts and gears.

A17. The types of fishing crafts are nets, boats/ships. Fishing gears include lines,
traps, wounding gears like spears, hooks etc.

Q18. What are the different types of chemical preservatives used for tissues in
genetic studies?
A18. For DNA analysis without PCR, tissues should be preserved fresh in buffer
solutions. For protein electrophoresis, tissues are preserved fresh or fresh frozen. For
DNA analysis with PCR, small amounts of tissues can be stored in ethanol.

Q19. What technique is used to determine the age of fishes?
A19. The age of fishes can be determined by counting the concentric ridges on scales
called circulii.

Q20. What is the importance of accurate species taxonomy and classification for
conservation efforts?
A20. Accurate taxonomy helps assess biodiversity correctly and identify threatened
species and populations for targeting conservation strategies.

Q21. What structures are found in the inner ear of fishes?
A21. The inner ear has three semicircular canals and three chambers - utriculus,
sacculus and lagena. Each chamber contains an otolith.

Q22. What adaptations help Labeo rohita survive as a herbivorous fish?
A22. Labeo rohita has a long convoluted intestine, absence of stomach, intestinal bulb
for storage and digestion of plant food.

   •   One ventricle – a muscular chamber that pumps blood to the gills for oxygenation

Focus on rays, skates, and sharks: Write the unique adaptations found in
Elasmobranchii. Discuss electroreception, cartilage-based skeletons, and their
ecological roles.

Elasmobranchii, the subclass encompassing sharks, rays, and skates, exhibits a suite of
distinctive adaptations that have enabled these fishes to thrive in marine environments for over
400 million years. Three of their most notable traits—electroreception, a cartilage-based
skeleton, and their varied ecological roles—work in concert to make elasmobranchs highly
effective predators, scavengers, and benthic engineers.

1. Electroreception
   •   Ampullae of Lorenzini
       Elasmobranchs possess hundreds to thousands of jelly-filled canals, the ampullae of
       Lorenzini, concentrated around their snouts and heads. Each canal opens to the skin
       surface via a pore and terminates in a cluster of sensory cells that detect minute electric
       potentials (as low as 5 nV/cm).
   •   Functions
           o Prey Detection: Buried or camouflaged prey emit bioelectric fields from muscle
               contractions and ion exchange. Sharks like the hammerhead use their wide
               cephalofoil to sweep the seafloor, pinpointing hidden rays beneath the sand.
           o Navigation & Orientation: Weak geomagnetic fields induce currents in the
               conductive seawater; elasmobranchs sense these to navigate long migrations with
               remarkable precision.
           o Social & Reproductive Cues: Some species may sense electrical signals
               produced during mating behaviors or territorial displays.

By converting electric signals into neural impulses, elasmobranchs gain a “sixth sense” that
complements vision and olfaction, especially valuable in low-light or turbid waters.

2. Cartilage-Based Skeleton
   •   Structural Composition
       Rather than bone, elasmobranchs’ endoskeletons consist of calcified cartilage—lighter,
       more flexible, and less dense than ossified bone. Mineralized “prisms” of calcium salts
       reinforce key regions (e.g., jaw joints, vertebral centra) without forfeiting pliability.
   •   Adaptive Advantages
           o Buoyancy & Energy Efficiency: A lighter skeleton reduces overall body density,
               helping sharks maintain depth without constantly swimming. Coupled with large
               oil-rich livers, this skeletal lightness lowers metabolic costs.
           o Flexibility & Maneuverability: Elastic cartilage allows powerful, whip-like
               movements of the tail (heterocercal in sharks) and pectoral fins (disc-shaped in

Elasmobranchs occupy diverse trophic niches—from apex predators to benthic foragers—

contains some glands which secrete these toxins. • Usually the body muscles are free of the toxin.
